blocks.text: Asia rose. The US slipped at the elite tier. Western Europe held its position. The 2024 methodology shifts were tectonic. Across the 2016 to 2026 decade, QS and Times Higher Education rank the same world differently and reset their methodologies on different cadences, yet the two systems converge on a single thesis: aggregate ranking composition has shifted faster than the headlines on individual institutions suggest, and the largest single-year movements of the decade are driven less by institutional performance than by the methodology rewrites both publishers shipped in 2024. The implication for decision-makers is uncomfortable but actionable: pillar-level diagnostics, the structural disagreement between the two systems, and the timing of methodology breaks now matter more than the year-on-year position of any single institution.

blocks.text: Greater China is the engine; the Gulf is now visible.

blocks.text: Reading the country data alone understates how concentrated the Asian gain is. Of the +24 Chinese institutions added to the THE Top 500 across the decade, the majority cluster at higher rank tiers than the average new entrant. Tsinghua, Peking, Fudan, Shanghai Jiao Tong, Zhejiang, and the University of Science and Technology of China have each entered or consolidated Top-100 positions. Greater China's THE Top 100 footprint tripled from 4 institutions to 12. The shift is broad enough that it cannot be attributed to one institution or one programme; it tracks the timing and intensity of China's Double First-Class Construction initiative, which replaced Project 985/211 in 2015.

blocks.text: The corollary deserves attention: the Asian rise has not displaced US institutions in equal measure. Mid-Top-100 public flagships, large and well-funded but operating in a more competitive citation environment, are where the erosion is concentrated.

blocks.text: The strategy mechanism is the most important part of the story. The UAE consolidated capability into a single research-intensive flagship and then funded it as a Vision 2071 priority asset. This is the Singapore playbook (NUS and NTU as twin flagships) at a one-flagship scale. It is a different model from Saudi Arabia's, which has spread investment more broadly across institutions, and a different model from Qatar's, where Top-500 footprint remains concentrated in Qatar University. The Khalifa rise has been faster than the Saudi institutional climb because consolidation compounds on existing infrastructure; the Saudi cohort grew on a wider base.

blocks.text: Country names are mapped to ISO-3166 alpha-3 codes via pycountry, with manual aliases for Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan, Iran, Korea, Russia, the UAE, and other commonly inconsistent entries.
